title: Language, identity and the sense of belonging
text:
Dialogue / 
	Opinion

Food For Thought Chair and Founder Varvara Athanasiou-Ioannou. Photo: Supplied

Varvara Athanasiou-Ioannou
		16 September 2026 12:30pm

This article is adapted from a speech delivered by Food For Thought Network Founder and Chair Varvara Athanasiou-Ioannou at the 12th Summer University in Sydney on 9 September 2026.

Athanasiou-Ioannou reflects on language, identity and belonging in the Greek diaspora, arguing that creating a sense of connection may be the first step towards encouraging future generations to reconnect with the Greek language.

Reflections from 25 years of the Food For Thought Network

I would like to begin with a question:

What is it that makes us feel Greek when we live thousands of kilometres away from Greece?

Is it language?

Is it our memories, our family, our traditions and our values?

Or is it something even deeper — the feeling that we belong somewhere?

Today’s presentation is experiential rather than academic.

I speak to you as an educator, author, migrant and volunteer, but above all as the founder of the Food For Thought Network, a network that for the past 25 years has been an important part of my life.

I came to Australia from Greece as a young woman, carrying with me a language, a culture and a deep sense of where I belonged.

Like many migrants, I learned to live between two worlds.

And through that journey, and through 25 years of connecting with women of the Greek diaspora, I began to think differently about the relationship between language, identity and belonging.

Perhaps language does not always create belonging first.

Perhaps, very often, belonging creates the desire to return to the language.

From language to belonging

Throughout my life, through education, writing and volunteering, I have been deeply committed to promoting Hellenism, the Greek language and Greek culture.

That commitment has never changed.

What changed was the way I began to understand how we can inspire people to embrace their cultural heritage.

When I founded the Food For Thought Network 25 years ago, I did not simply want to create another Greek organisation.

I wanted to create a space where women of Greek heritage, and their friends, could meet, exchange ideas and experiences, learn, build relationships and, most importantly, feel that they belonged. That their voices mattered.

Over its 25-year journey, FFTN has organised more than 160 events.

This journey also led to the creation of my book, “HER VOICE: Greek Women and Their Friends,” which shares 42 personal stories of women.

And in 2024, in Ioannina, we organised the first Global Women & Hellenism Conference, bringing together women from Greece and the Greek diaspora around the world.

Through all these experiences, I began to notice something:

In our experience, language was often not the starting point. It was the result of connection.

The reality of the diaspora

For those of us living in the diaspora, the relationship with language and identity is not always simple.

Many second- and third-generation women grew up at a time when assimilation was often seen as the pathway to success.

Some had negative experiences at Greek school.

Many understood Greek but did not feel comfortable speaking it.

Some felt that their Greek was “not good enough.”

And this made me ask:

Should we measure someone’s relationship with their Greek identity by how well they speak Greek?

I believe we should not.

The question for me became:

How do we create an environment where people want to reconnect with their heritage?

At the Food For Thought Network, our meetings are mainly conducted in English, because this is the language in which many women feel most comfortable.

We talk about issues that matter to their lives: leadership, health, relationships, professional development, social and cultural issues.

And then something happened that I had not planned.

As the women got to know each other better, as friendships and trust developed,

Greek slowly began to return.

A Greek word.

A childhood memory.

A story about their grandmother.

A familiar expression.

Not always perfect Greek.

But authentic Greek.

And that is when I realised:

We cannot force people to learn a language.

But we can create a space where they want to  speak it.

Three women – three journeys

Let me give you three very brief examples.

Kalli grew up in South Australia. She had some exposure to the Greek language, but had not developed a particularly strong connection with her Greek heritage.

Through her involvement with FFTN and the opportunity to speak about her scientific work, she began to recognise that her Greek identity could coexist with her professional identity.

She became more interested in the language, her family history, Greece and Cyprus. Eventually, she also obtained a Greek passport.

Her journey did not begin with language. It began with belonging.

Maria, a second-generation Greek Australian, began as a young adult to search for a deeper connection with the community and her Greek heritage.

Gradually, language became a form of creative expression.

She began writing poetry in Greek and later taught Greek in Saturday schools.

Connection became expression — and eventually transmission to the next generation.

And Despina offers us a different perspective.

Born and raised in Australia by Greek immigrant parents, she grew up with both an Australian way of life and a strong Greek cultural foundation.

Later, living and working in Switzerland, China and Greece, she found that different aspects of these cultures reinforced values she had already grown up with: the emphasis on education and continuous improvement in China, transparency and responsibility in Switzerland, and language, family, religion and traditions in Greece.

These experiences strengthened her sense of belonging, but also showed her that cultures can sometimes meet and complement one another, while at other times creating a sense of dissonance.

Her story reminds us that cultural identity is not something we leave behind when we cross borders.

We carry it with us — and it continues to evolve.

Despina also remained connected with FFTN online and offered to become a mentor.

Identity is not necessarily limited by geography.

From Australia to the world

This became even clearer during the pandemic.

We created the Greek Women and Friends Global Forum, and suddenly our community became global.

Women from Australia, Greece and other countries were meeting online.

And naturally, our conversations began moving between Greek and English — what we often call Greeklish.

Some spoke Greek.

Others spoke English.

And many moved naturally from one language to the other.

Gradually, I began inviting some speakers to present in Greek, particularly when they were sharing personal stories.

And something began to change.

Some women began choosing for themselves to present in Greek.

We saw this also at the Global Women & Hellenism Conference in Ioannina.

And for me, there is a huge difference between:

“I have to speak Greek”

and

“I want to speak Greek.”

The first comes from obligation.

The second comes from connection.

And what about the next generation?

And here, I believe, lies perhaps our greatest challenge for the future.

What does all this mean for the third and fourth generations of the Greek diaspora?

For a young person who may be born in Sydney or Melbourne, study in another country, work in a global environment and communicate every day through technology with people all around the world?

Perhaps we can no longer understand Greek identity only through geography — or even only through language proficiency.

Perhaps we need to create spaces where young people can discover their own relationship with their Greek heritage.

Without the fear that their Greek is not good enough.

Without feeling that they have to prove how Greek they are.

But with curiosity, connection and pride.

Belonging is the soil

After 25 years, what do I take away from this journey?

That language is one of the strongest carriers of memory, culture and identity.

But my experience in the diaspora has also taught me something else:

Identity cannot be imposed. It is cultivated through relationships.

I often think of it this way:

Belonging is the soil.

Language is the flower.

We cannot make a flower grow by pulling at it.

We need to nurture the soil.

We need to create the environment in which it can take root, grow and blossom.

Perhaps, therefore, when we talk about the future of the Greek language in the diaspora, we should not only ask:

“How will we make our children speak Greek?”

Perhaps we should first ask:

“Do they feel connected to their Greek heritage?”

“Do they feel that there is a place for them within our community?”

“Have we given them a reason to want to return to the language?”

Because these 25 years have taught me something very simple:

We did not create a community because we spoke Greek.

We began speaking Greek because we created a community where people felt they belonged.
